Have you seen the headline this morning? Harbor Capital and Northgate are going to merge.
I saw it on my way in. When was it announced?
At seven. It was decided behind closed doors last week, and the shareholders were told last night.
Were any of our clients affected?
Two of them. Both of their accounts are managed by Northgate at the moment.
And who is in charge now? Was a new director appointed?
Not yet. A name is expected in the spring, so nothing is changed for now.
Then I will call both clients today, before they read it in the news.
The decision was made last week.
Our clients were told before the public.

Read any business headline and you will notice something strange. Rates were raised. Jobs were cut. A new director was appointed. Nobody seems to do anything, and things simply happen. That is the passive, and journalists use it for a simple reason: in the news, what happened is more interesting than who did it. Sometimes the person is not important. Sometimes everybody already knows who it was. And sometimes, honestly, nobody wants to say. When you do need the person, add by and the name, as in the deal was approved by the board. But most of the time you do not need it, and the sentence is cleaner without it. So the next time you explain a decision to a client, start with the decision, not with the people in the meeting.

Good morning, and here is the business news at eight. Harbor Capital and Northgate Bank are going to merge, it was announced this morning. The deal was approved by both boards on Thursday, and shareholders were told by letter last night. The new bank will be called Harbor Northgate, and its main office will stay in New York. A new chief executive was not named, and no decision about jobs was made. In other news, interest rates were raised again yesterday, for the third time this year. And the price of coffee was cut at two of the biggest chains in the country. That is all for now. More at nine.
